crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories are research systems in which software plans experiments, robotic hardware runs them, and the measured results feed back into the next round of planning without a person moving samples between steps.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: Digital twins for experiments are software replicas of a physical experimental setup, kept in step with the real instrument through a stream of measurements.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data covers the readings produced by laboratory hardware, from spectrophotometers and chromatographs to temperature probes, pressure transducers and environmental monitors.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols covers the use of computational methods to improve the design, scheduling and execution of wet lab procedures.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies covers the prediction of when a laboratory will run out of consumables, reagents, and other stocked items, and how much of each will be needed over a coming period.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation covers the machinery and software that let experiments run with less human hands-on time and more machine-readable record keeping. Artificial intelligence is doing concrete work here: scheduling robotic liquid handlers, choosing the next batch of conditions to test, reading instrument output, and flagging runs that look wrong before they waste a week. Self-driving labs close the loop, so a model proposes an experiment, a robot runs it, and the result feeds back into the next proposal. Digital twins mirror a physical experiment or instrument in software so parameters can be tried without consuming reagents. None of this replaces the scientist, it changes what the scientist spends the day on.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The pieces that work reliably are narrow: liquid handling, plate reading, and closed-loop optimisation over a small, well-defined parameter space. What is not solved is the messy middle, where instruments speak different formats, samples degrade, and a protocol that worked on Tuesday fails on Thursday for reasons nobody logged. Digital twins are only as good as the physical model behind them, and many are calibrated on too little data to be trusted far from the conditions they were built on. Supply forecasting is genuinely hard because it depends on vendor behaviour and shipping, not just on the lab's own history. The honest limit is that autonomy is local, and most labs still need a person to notice when the loop has quietly gone wrong.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from hardware to planning. Self-Driving Laboratories is the widest view, describing how sensing, decision making and robotics combine into a loop, and it is the place to start if you want the whole picture. Digital Twins for Experiments narrows to the software mirror of a single setup, useful when you want to test a change without touching the bench. Instrument and Sensor Data sits underneath both, because every loop depends on clean readings, and it is where you go when the numbers themselves are the problem. Optimising Lab Protocols takes those readings and asks how to change the procedure, which is the step most people mean when they say the lab is learning. Forecasting Lab Supplies looks outward to what the lab will need and when, closing the section on the logistics that keep the other four running.
